questions.scenario: An endpoint lists 500 active accounts with each customer's name. SQL logs show one select from account, then 500 nearly identical `select ... from customer where id=?` statements.
questions.question: What is this, and which fix loads the data in one query?
options: Connection pool exhaustion; raise the pool size
The N+1 select problem; use a fetch join (join fetch a.customer), an @EntityGraph, or a DTO projection
questions.explanation: Each lazy access fires its own query. Fetching the association in the original query (or projecting the needed columns) turns 501 round trips into one.

questions.scenario: A product enum is reordered (`CURRENT` moved before `SAVINGS`). Afterwards, every savings account displays as current.
questions.question: What mapping caused this, and what should be used?
options: Enums can't be persisted; use strings
questions.explanation: ORDINAL stores 0, 1, 2, which changes meaning when the enum changes. STRING stores the constant's name and is stable.

questions.scenario: `TransferService.transferAll()` loops and calls `this.transfer(...)`, which is annotated @Transactional. Logs show that no transaction is ever started: a failure between the debit and the credit leaves the debit saved.
questions.question: Why didn't @Transactional apply?
options: Self-invocation bypasses the Spring proxy, so the annotation on transfer() is never applied when called from inside the same bean
questions.explanation: Transactional behaviour is added by a proxy around the bean. Internal this.method() calls don't go through it. Move the method to another bean or put the transaction on the outer method.

questions.scenario: A service method annotated @Transactional throws a checked `StatementGenerationException` after inserting rows. The rows remain in the database.
questions.question: Why?
options: By default Spring rolls back only on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error); use an unchecked exception or rollbackFor
The exception was thrown too late
questions.explanation: Spring's default mirrors EJB conventions: checked exceptions commit. Prefer unchecked domain exceptions, or configure rollbackFor explicitly.

questions.scenario: Two back-office agents edit the same customer profile. The second save silently overwrites the first agent's changes.
questions.question: Which JPA feature detects this conflict?
options: A @Version field (optimistic locking); the stale update fails with an optimistic-locking exception you can map to 409
questions.explanation: @Version adds 'AND version = ?' to the UPDATE. If someone else committed first, no row matches and Hibernate throws, instead of losing an update.

questions.scenario: A developer sets `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update` in production 'so new columns appear automatically'.
questions.question: What should the team do instead?
options: Manage the schema with Flyway (or Liquibase) migrations and set ddl-auto=validate so startup fails on mismatches
Use none and edit the database by hand
Keep update but back up daily
questions.explanation: update makes unreviewed, unversioned, sometimes destructive schema changes and can't handle renames or data migrations. Migrations are reviewed and repeatable; validate catches drift.

questions.scenario: A statement endpoint returns `account.getTransactions()` (a @OneToMany collection) as JSON. For a 6-year-old business account, it takes 40 seconds and uses gigabytes of memory.
questions.question: What is the better design?
options: Query transactions with a paged, filtered repository method (ideally a DTO projection) instead of loading the whole collection
questions.explanation: Unbounded collections should be queried, not navigated. A paged projection loads only the requested page of columns.

questions.scenario: You're reviewing a new JPA entity class.
questions.question: Which of these are problems?
options: toString() prints the lazy accounts collection
It has a protected no-arg constructor
questions.explanation: Final classes prevent Hibernate's proxies; toString on lazy associations triggers loading (or LazyInitializationException); @ManyToOne defaults to EAGER. A protected no-arg constructor is correct.
